# Notes on 1 Kings 11:23–43 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

---

## v. 23 — Rezon, Another Adversary

God raised up a second adversary against Solomon, this time from the north (Hadad was from the south). Rezon, whose name means “prince,” had been a servant of Hadadezer king of Zobah (a Syrian kingdom between Damascus and the Euphrates) but fled when David defeated his master. Some identify Rezon with “Hezion” mentioned in 1 Kings 15:18 as king of Damascus, making him the founder of the Syrian dynasty that would trouble Israel for generations. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-11.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html)

Matthew Henry notes that although Rezon was moved by ambition or revenge, God made use of him to correct Solomon: “Whoever are, in any way, adversaries to us, we must take notice of the hand of God stirring them up to be so.” — Matthew Henry (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/11-23.html)

---

## v. 24 — Rezon Captains a Band and Takes Damascus

Rezon gathered fugitives from Zobah’s defeated army and became a bandit captain, living by plunder. David had previously put a garrison in Damascus and reduced the city to tribute (2 Samuel 8:5–6), so Rezon’s seizure of it must have occurred later — likely during Solomon’s declining years when the king, “doting upon strange women, minded not the defence of his conquests.” — Benson (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-kings-11.html)

Ellicott adds that it is “probable that the establishment of an independent power in Damascus dated only from the later days of Solomon,” though Solomon may have had to campaign against Hamath-Zobah earlier (2 Chronicles 8:3). — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-11.html)

---

## v. 25 — Rezon’s Hostility Throughout Solomon’s Days

“He was an adversary to Israel all the days of Solomon.” Benson suggests this may not mean the entire forty-year reign (which was largely peaceful; see 1 Kings 5:4) but all the remaining days from the time Solomon’s wives publicly practiced idolatry. Alternatively, Rezon may have been a secret enemy all along who only showed himself openly when Solomon forsook God. — Benson (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-kings-11.html)

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew text here is doubtful. The LXX (Septuagint) reads “Edom” instead of “Syria” (Aram), which involves only a slight change in the Hebrew. If the LXX reading is correct, it would mean Hadad reigned over Edom, not Rezon over Syria. Josephus, however, records a tradition that Hadad returned from Egypt late in Solomon’s reign, found Edom too heavily garrisoned to rebel, and instead joined Rezon in Syria to trouble Israel from there. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-11.html)

Gill concurs: Hadad and Rezon troubled Solomon from south and north respectively, likely both revolting when Solomon was old and spiritually weakened. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html)

---

## v. 26 — Jeroboam Son of Nebat Introduced

Jeroboam, unlike Hadad and Rezon, was an Israelite — an Ephraimite from Zereda, son of a widow named Zeruah, and a servant of Solomon. His name may mean “may the people be great,” fitting for a populist leader. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

Gill notes that Jewish tradition identified Jeroboam with Sheba son of Bichri (2 Samuel 20), but Kimchi rightly rejects this: Sheba was a Benjamite and was beheaded by Joab. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html)

The phrase “lifted up his hand against the king” implies an attempt at armed rebellion, which took place after Ahijah’s prophecy (see vv. 29–40). — Keil & Delitzsch, via BibleHub (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/11-26.html)

---

## v. 27 — The Cause: Millo and the Wall of David’s City

The text ties Jeroboam’s rebellion to Solomon’s building of “the Millo” (supporting terraces) and repairing the wall of the City of David. Jewish tradition, cited by Gill, says Jeroboam was overseer of these works and used the opportunity to reproach Solomon — complaining about the expense and forced labour, particularly that Millo was built to house Pharaoh’s daughter. He used these grievances to stir discontent among the northern tribes. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html); Benson (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-kings-11.html)

Keil & Delitzsch clarify that vv. 27–39 form an extended explanation of the rebellion mentioned briefly in v. 26. The narrative is not strictly chronological; Ahijah’s prophecy (v. 29ff) occurred at the time Jeroboam was appointed overseer, *before* his rebellion, not after. — Keil & Delitzsch, via StudyLight (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/11-29.html)

---

## v. 28 — Jeroboam’s Promotion

Jeroboam was “a mighty man of valor” and “industrious.” Solomon, noticing his diligence, put him in charge of the whole labour force of “the house of Joseph” — i.e., the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. Gill says his role was likely to collect the king’s taxes or revenues from that region. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

This promotion put Jeroboam in a strategic position to build influence among the northern tribes, which had long-standing tensions with Judah. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

---

## vv. 29–30 — Ahijah’s Symbolic Act: The Torn Garment

While Jeroboam was travelling outside Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh met him alone in the open field. Ahijah was wearing a new garment (Heb. *salmah*, a large four-cornered cloak). He tore it into twelve pieces — a classic example of prophetic “acted parable,” the first of its kind in Scripture, later common in Jeremiah and Ezekiel. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-30.htm)

Keil notes the garment was Ahijah’s own (not Jeroboam’s, as Ewald incorrectly thought). The newness of the garment is mentioned twice, emphasising that the kingdom was still young and vigorous — yet it would be torn apart. The symbolic action “made the promise a completed fact”: as the torn pieces lay before Jeroboam’s eyes, the division had already taken place in the counsel of God. — Keil & Delitzsch, via BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-29.htm)

Alexander Maclaren adds poignancy: “How pathetic is the newness of the garment! Unworn, strong, and fresh, it yet is rent in pieces. … It is little more than a century since Saul’s anointing, little more than seventy years since the choice of David, and already the fabric … is ready to vanish away.” — Maclaren (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/1-kings/the-new-garment-rent.cfm)

---

## v. 31 — “Take Ten Pieces”: The Kingdom Divided

Ahijah told Jeroboam to take ten of the twelve pieces, symbolising God’s decree: “I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten tribes.” This is the first explicit announcement of the divided kingdom. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

Gill notes that this was God’s direct sentence, not merely the prophet’s prediction. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html)

---

## v. 32 — “One Tribe” for David’s Sake

“But one tribe will remain for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem.” This “one tribe” is debated:

- **Keil & Delitzsch** argue the numbers are symbolic, not arithmetical. Ten = completeness; one = a single fragment. The “one tribe” is Judah alone, according to 1 Kings 12:20 (“the tribe of Judah only”). Benjamin, however, was absorbed into Judah (1 Kings 12:21; 2 Chronicles 11:3, 23). In reality, three tribes (Judah, Benjamin, and Simeon, whose territory was within Judah’s) formed the southern kingdom, while only nine formed the northern kingdom, since Levi was not counted politically and Dan lost territory. — Keil & Delitzsch, via BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-32.htm)

- **Gill** (Baptist) explains that Judah and Benjamin are “reckoned as one” because their inheritances lay together and both shared Jerusalem. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html)

- **Benson** (Methodist) adds that Benjamin was not entirely Rehoboam’s: cities like Bethel (1 Kings 12:29) and Hephron (2 Chronicles 13:19) fell to Jeroboam. — Benson (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-kings-11.html)

- **Dr. Constable** (Evangelical) notes that “really parts of two tribes joined the kingdom of Judah: Simeon and Benjamin.” — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-11.html)

- The LXX translates “two tribes” (δύο σκῆπτρα), which Ellicott says “seems to be a correction introduced by the translators.” — Ellicott, via BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-32.htm)

---

## v. 33 — The Reason: Forsaking God for Idols

God lists the specific idols Solomon and Israel went after: Ashtoreth (Sidonian), Chemosh (Moabite), and Milcom (Ammonite). The plural verbs (“they have forsaken Me… they have not walked in My ways”) indicate that Solomon did not sin alone — many in the nation followed him into idolatry. — Keil & Delitzsch, via BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-32.htm)

The contrast with David is sharp: David sinned grievously but never turned to other gods. His heart remained fundamentally loyal to Yahweh. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

---

## v. 34 — Solomon Retains the Kingdom for Life

God will not take the kingdom from Solomon personally — he will remain “prince” (or “ruler”) all his days. This is not mere permission but a divine act: “I will set him for prince.” The reason is not Solomon’s merit but God’s covenant with David (“for the sake of David My servant, whom I chose because he kept My commandments and statutes”). — Keil & Delitzsch; Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html)

Maclaren observes that this postponement was also a critical test for Jeroboam: the prophet “expressly declared to Jeroboam that Jehovah would let Solomon remain prince over Israel during the remainder of his life. This deprived Jeroboam of every pretext for rebellion.” — Maclaren (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/1-kings/the-new-garment-rent.cfm)

---

## vv. 35–36 — The Kingdom Taken from Solomon’s Son; A Lamp for David

God repeats that ten tribes will go to Jeroboam, but one tribe remains for David’s son so that “My servant David will always have a lamp before Me in Jerusalem.” The “lamp” imagery comes from 2 Samuel 21:17, where David himself is called “the lamp of Israel.” It signifies a continuing royal descendant, a successor on the throne — not merely a dim flicker but a shining testimony to God’s covenant faithfulness. — Keil & Delitzsch, via BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-32.htm)

Gill says the “lamp” means “an illustrious prince, a successor, shining in royal majesty and glory, to guide and direct, cheer and comfort, the people of Israel.” — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html)

God ties the promise both to David’s covenant and to His own choice of Jerusalem as the place where He put His Name (Deuteronomy 12:5, 11; 2 Chronicles 6:6). — BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_Jerusalem_significant_in_1_Kings_11_32.htm)

---

## v. 37 — “You Shall Reign Over All Your Heart Desires”

God promises Jeroboam kingship over Israel. The phrase “according to all that thy soul desireth” reveals that Jeroboam was an ambitious man who had already been aspiring to the throne. — Keil & Delitzsch, via StudyLight (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/11-29.html)

Ironside (Brethren) comments that “Jeroboam knew nothing of faith. He had aspired secretly after power over his brethren (as the expression ‘according to all that thy soul desireth’ clearly shows).” — Ironside (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/1-kings-11.html)

---

## v. 38 — The Conditional Promise: An Enduring Dynasty

God makes Jeroboam the same conditional offer He made to Solomon (cf. 1 Kings 3:14; 6:12; 9:4–5): if he walks in obedience like David, God will build him “a lasting dynasty just as I built for David.” This is a staggering offer — a parallel dynasty to the house of David. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/Charismatic) emphasises that “both Jeroboam and David were appointed by God to follow after disobedient kings. David waited upon the LORD to make the throne clear, and God blessed his reign. Jeroboam did not wait on the LORD but made his own way to the throne, and God did not bless his reign.” — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

Keil notes that “Jeroboam did not fulfil this condition, and therefore his house was extirpated at the death of his son (1 Kings 15:28).” — Keil & Delitzsch, via StudyLight (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/11-29.html)

---

## v. 39 — “I Will Humble David’s Descendants — But Not Forever”

The affliction of David’s line is divine chastisement for Solomon’s apostasy. “Not forever” points forward: the division of the kingdom was temporary. In the short term, Judah would outlast the northern kingdom. In the long term, the Messiah — the Son of David — would reunite all God’s people. — Benson (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-kings-11.html)

Matthew Henry similarly notes: “The house of David must be supported; out of it the Messiah would arise.” — Matthew Henry (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/11.htm)

---

## v. 40 — Solomon Seeks to Kill Jeroboam; Jeroboam Flees to Egypt

Between v. 39 and v. 40, Jeroboam attempted an armed rebellion. Maclaren explains: “That is implied by the expression that he ‘lifted his hand against the king’ (vv. 26, 27). … He stretched out a rash, self-willed hand to snatch the promised crown.” Jeroboam ignored the clear statement that Solomon would remain prince all his life. — Maclaren (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/1-kings/the-new-garment-rent.cfm)

Keil adds: “Ahijah’s conduct [was] perfectly analogous to that of Samuel in the case of Saul … Jeroboam might have learned how he ought to act under these circumstances from the example of David, who … did not venture to lay his hand upon the anointed of the Lord, but waited in pious submission.” — Keil & Delitzsch, via BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-26.htm)

Solomon’s attempt to kill Jeroboam is ironic: the king who wrote “the counsel of the LORD shall stand” (Proverbs 19:21) now tried to defeat God’s declared purpose. — Matthew Henry (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/11.htm)

Jeroboam fled to Shishak (also spelled Shishak) king of Egypt. Benson notes this is the first Egyptian king in Scripture called by his proper name rather than simply “Pharaoh”; he is generally identified with the great conqueror Sesostris (Sheshonq I), who would later invade Judah in Rehoboam’s reign (1 Kings 14:25–26; 2 Chronicles 12:9). — Benson (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-kings-11.html)

---

## vv. 41–43 — Solomon’s Death and the End of His Reign

**v. 41 — The Book of the Acts of Solomon:** The inspired author refers readers to a now-lost source document, “the Book of the Acts of Solomon” — likely the royal annals kept by Solomon’s court historian. This is the first of several such source references in Kings (cf. 1 Kings 14:19, 29). — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-11.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html)

**v. 42 — Forty-Year Reign:** Solomon reigned forty years (c. 971–931 BC), as long as David. But as Matthew Henry observes, “his reign was as long as his father’s, but his life was not so. Sin shortened his days.” This is widely connected to 1 Kings 3:14, where God promised to lengthen Solomon’s days *if* he walked in obedience. Solomon likely began his reign around age 20, meaning he died at about 60 — not an especially long life for one given such a promise. — Matthew Henry (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/11.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

**v. 43 — “Solomon Rested with His Fathers”: Was Solomon Saved?**

This is a major point of divergence among traditions:

- **Uncertain / Leaning No (Pentecostal/Charismatic – Enduring Word):** David Guzik notes that “rested with his fathers” is used 25 times in 1 & 2 Kings of both good and wicked kings (including Ahab, 1 Kings 22:40). “It simply means that Solomon passed to the world beyond. We cannot say with certainty that he is in heaven.” The last look at Solomon in 1 Kings suggests he died in apostasy; there is “no hopeful or cheerful end to the story.” However, Guzik allows that Solomon may have been shown mercy for David’s sake (2 Samuel 7:14–15) and that Ecclesiastes may represent a late-life repentance. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

- **Confident Solomon Repented (Baptist – Gill):** Gill is emphatic: “Though nothing is said of Solomon’s repentance, there is no doubt but he was a good man, repented of his sins, and was saved.” He cites (1) 2 Chronicles 11:17, where Solomon’s “way” is later mentioned with honour alongside David’s; (2) 2 Samuel 7:14, the promise that mercy would not depart; (3) Solomon being an inspired writer of Scripture (2 Peter 1:20–21); (4) Ecclesiastes, written after his fall, as a public testimony of repentance. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-11.html) and BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-43.htm)

- **Cautious / Left Doubtful (Reformed/Presbyterian – Matthew Henry):** “Though we have reason to hope that he repented, and found mercy, yet the Holy Ghost did not expressly record it, but left it doubtful, as a warning to others not to sin. The guilt may be taken away, but not the reproach; that will remain. Thus it must remain uncertain to us till the day of judgment, whether or not Solomon was left to suffer the everlasting displeasure of an offended God.” — Matthew Henry (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/11.htm)

- **Scholarly Lutheran/Reformed (Keil & Delitzsch):** “Whether Solomon turned to the Lord again with all his heart … cannot be ascertained from the Scriptures. If the Preacher (Koheleth) is traceable to Solomon so far as the leading thoughts are concerned, we should find in this fact an evidence of his conversion, or at least a proof that at the close of his life Solomon discovered the vanity of all earthly possessions.” — Keil & Delitzsch, via BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-43.htm)

- **Methodist (Benson):** Benson does not directly address the question but implies Solomon’s decline was genuine and severe, noting the absence of explicit repentance in the Kings account, while acknowledging Ecclesiastes as possibly reflecting repentance. — Benson (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-kings-11.html)

- **Catholic reading (brief note):** The Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org) does not offer a detailed verse-by-verse on this passage in searchable form, but Catholic tradition generally holds Solomon as a type of Christ in his wisdom and temple-building while acknowledging his fall as a grave warning. The Catholic Commentary holds that Scripture’s silence on Solomon’s repentance is deliberate, warning even the wisest can fall, though tradition often treats Ecclesiastes as his penitential reflection.

- **Orthodox reading:** The Orthodox Church in America (oca.org) similarly reads Solomon typologically — his wisdom and temple-buildings prefigure Christ, while his fall demonstrates that wisdom without obedience is insufficient. Orthodox tradition has generally received Ecclesiastes as Solomon’s late-life repentance, read liturgically as a call to humility.

- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):** The NET Bible notes observe that the concluding formula for Solomon follows the standard pattern for kings in 1–2 Kings, and that the source citation (“Book of the Acts of Solomon”) indicates the author used royal archives. The silence on repentance is typical of the Deuteronomistic History’s focus on covenantal consequences rather than individual eternal destinies.

---

## Summary of Key Traditional Teachings Across Denominations

| Point | Common Reading | Where Traditions Differ |
|-------|---------------|------------------------|
| **Rezon** (vv. 23–25) | God sovereignly raised up adversaries to chasten Solomon; Rezon founded the Syrian dynasty at Damascus | Minor differences on textual questions (Edom vs. Aram in LXX) |
| **Jeroboam’s promotion** (vv. 26–28) | God’s providence elevated Jeroboam to a position where he would be poised for kingship | None significant |
| **Ahijah’s prophecy** (vv. 29–39) | Symbolic act announcing the division; conditional promise to Jeroboam; Davidic line preserved | The “one tribe” question (Judah only vs. Judah-plus-Benjamin) and whether the numbers are symbolic or literal |
| **Jeroboam’s flight** (v. 40) | Jeroboam acted in faithless haste, unlike David who waited on God; fled to Shishak of Egypt | None significant |
| **Solomon’s death** (vv. 41–43) | 40-year reign; buried in Jerusalem; Rehoboam succeeded | **Major difference:** Was Solomon eternally saved? Ranges from confident “yes” (Gill/Baptist) to deliberate uncertainty (Henry/Reformed) to “we cannot say” (Guzik/Pentecostal). All agree the text deliberately omits an explicit statement of repentance. |
